en: *Īśvaravādimataparīkṣā*.

Under the title *Anekāntavādanirāsa*, Iyengar (cited above), pp. 81–85, has edited a text by Jitāri which is designated in its colophon as the *Digambaramataparīkṣā*. It begins: "Now the doctrine of the Ārhats is examined; here these Digambaras describe the aggregate of entities (*bhāvagrāma*) as consisting of arising, persistence, and dissolution, in the form of substance and modification (*dravyaparyāya*)."
...In the present collection, there is now found a text that has a very similar structure, though its title has not been preserved. It comprises folios IIB.

Following the *Digambaramataparīkṣā*, the *Īśvaravādimataparīkṣā* is here proposed as a tentative title.
Bühnemann 1982, p. [number].
Now the doctrine of the proponents of a Lord (Īśvara) is examined.
Here, these Naiyāyikas and others declare that all effects, such as trees and so forth, are created by a Lord.
What, then, is the means of valid cognition for them in that case?
It is inference; for it is observed that whatever is an effect is invariably concomitant with an agent.
Just as an effect such as a jar [is produced by a maker], so too is the tree and other objects that are the subject of dispute;
and he who is that maker is the Blessed Lord Īśvara.
Regarding "tanvādi" [or] "tunvādi," it is said here:
MS °tunvādi°. MS atrocyate.

If the mere fact of being an effect were established as having an invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*) with an intelligent cause, then from the observation of the state of being an effect, one could infer that trees and other such things have an intelligent cause; however, this very concomitance is impossible to establish. For instance, objects such as grass and the like are seen to arise even without the intervention of human activity.
How, then, could a person acting with foresight determine that every effect is produced by a person?
How could one [determine] that [the world] consists of bodies and so forth?
...is considered [to be] by the agent... MS ...to cause to go.

In this regard, [the opponent objects]: "But surely, those effects whose production is seen to occur without human activity, as well as those whose production is seen [to require it]— all such things, from grass and the like up to mountains and the like— are indeed included within the subject of the proposition."
Furthermore, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) within the subject (*pakṣa*) is not tenable;

for in some cases, it is impossible to apprehend the pervasion because the pervader is imperceptible, and in other cases, it would follow that inference could never occur because the very means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the pervasion is unestablished.
Therefore, just as the pervasion of smoke by fire is perceived in places such as a kitchen, so too here the pervasion of an effect by an intelligent cause is perceived in things such as a jar.

Or rather, just as a person who has grasped the pervasion elsewhere infers fire upon seeing smoke on a mountain and so forth, so too one might infer a creator from the observation of being an effect in grass and such; thus, there is nothing at all that is untenable.
°dhayaś MS sāntigra° MS °māṇe so° MS
That is incorrect;
for it has been stated that the world, observing grass and other things arising even without human activity, does not perceive the pervasion that every effect whatsoever is preceded by a person.

In this regard, we do not perceive what kind of resolution has been offered by this person who, with his ears and heart, says that "all things, including grass and so forth, have been made the subject of the proposition (pakṣīkṛta) by us.
For if smoke were seen arising even without fire, would anyone then apprehend its pervasion (vyāpti) from that? No.
abandoned; cf. 39.10ff. is [so] designated.
Now, if it is thought that this particular person is invisible and beyond the senses,
and therefore even grass and other things produced preceded by his activity are not perceived as such; [then we reply:]...
Furthermore, non-perception of the unobservable does not prove the non-existence of an object;

therefore, even if grass and the like are not perceived to be preceded by a person, they do not thereby possess the status of being non-human (apauruṣeya), because there would be no apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). [End of] MS. Atīndriyaḥ.
This too is incorrect,
because in this case, grass and so forth are not perceived as being preceded by human activity.
And let that [causality] not be perceived because the person is invisible or non-existent— what is the use of this investigation?
In any case, someone who does not perceive any effect whatsoever to be preceded by a person understands the lack of pervasion (avyāpti) of effects in general by means of a person.
And if pervasion is not understood, how can there even be talk of inference?
asravaka° MS anumāna° MS It might be argued as follows:
If an effect such as a jar were not preceded by an intelligent agent, it would likewise not exist;
for it does not arise even once from a causeless source.
Therefore, perceiving that even a single effect has a person as its cause, one concludes—due to the absence of any distinction—that every effect whatsoever is preceded by an intelligent agent.
The claim that "just as one perceiving smoke caused by fire in a kitchen concludes all smoke to have that as its cause" is also untenable,
because the absence of any distinction [between the two cases] remains unproven.
For indeed, effects such as jars, which are dependent on a person (puruṣa), are seen to be of one kind, whereas this effect consisting of atoms, trees, and so forth, is of another kind; thus,
the mere assertion that they are "the same" is nothing but idle chatter.
Therefore, at the time of the cognition of pervasion, such a case is indeed rejected;

for no one, while cognizing smoke as being pervaded by fire, would—merely because of the commonality of being denotable by the word "smoke"—cognize even a painted smoke as being pervaded by fire. (MS)
Now, is it not the case that even a jar and the like are called an "effect" because they exist when their cause exists?

Since trees and the like also exist when their causes are present and are thus fit for the conventional designation of "effect," there is no distinction between the subject of dispute and its opposite in terms of being an effect; therefore, just as the state of being preceded by an intelligent agent is established in one case, that same state should be recognized everywhere.
To this it is replied:

since smoke and non-smoke are also indistinguishable insofar as they are both effects, then for the "Beloved of the Gods" (devānāmpriya), the inference that every effect has fire as its cause— based on the cognition that the effect which is smoke is caused by fire— would likewise result [absurdly].

Now, if you think that it is not merely an effect (*kāryamātra*) that is understood as being pervaded by mere fire (*vahnimātra*), but rather a specific effect, namely smoke (*dhūma*), and that for this reason alone its inference [of fire] occurs and not from a mere effect—then why is it that a mere effect is not perceived as being pervaded by fire, just as it is perceived as being pervaded by a person (*puruṣa*)? To this very point it is said:
for in that case too, this can be asserted.
If no effect whatsoever were preceded by fire, then smoke too would not be preceded by fire,
because that which lacks a cause does not produce [its effect] even once.
If it is argued that because another effect is seen to arise even without fire, there is no pervasion of all effects by fire— then in that case,
since grass and the like are also seen to arise without a person, it would likewise be impossible to ascertain that all effects are pervaded by a person.

Now, whatever kind of effect is perceived as preceded by that [cause] through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), that very kind is determined to be pervaded by it; thus, inference is to be sought from the mere effect (*kāryamātra*).
This is to be supplied because of the term *tadvyāptam* and because of the term *puruṣapūrvakam* in the following sentence.
(The reading is *°mātrad* according to the manuscript.)

In that case, one must necessarily admit—even if unwillingly—that only such an effect as is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be preceded by a person is determined to be pervaded by him; therefore, there can be no inference of a person from every kind of effect. Furthermore, it must be accepted that effects such as pots and the like are understood to follow the positive and negative concomitance of a person, whereas trees and the like—which produce the cognition of being "made" even in those who have never seen them being made—are dissimilar to [human-made] effects.

And in the absence of [a reason] that excludes what is the subject of dispute, if there were a difference of another kind, then—just like a temple or similar structures seen in an empty city—even trees and the like would not necessarily allow for the inference of a creator distinct from ourselves. *Note:
The final line of manuscript 1/2 is obscured by the upper portion of the following folio.*
vaiśyaḥ MS °tvā MS °dātīvi° MS.
The negation is redundant. Delete *na* in *nāsmād°*.
Now, if it is asserted that the creator of trees and so forth is distinct from ourselves and others precisely because he is invisible:
That too is not logical;
for the proponents of God as the cause do not maintain that there is a difference between the pot and the tree merely on the basis of their being visible or invisible.
Because invisible beings such as *piśācas* are possible,
it cannot be asserted that the very person who creates trees and so forth— who is invisible to people like us— is indeed the Lord (*īśvara*).
For what they intend by "the Great Lord" is a specific kind of person who is skilled in the creation of the universe and knows the ultimate reality of all things.
Furthermore, even if it were established that [trees] have an invisible creator as their antecedent, the fact that trees of the same genus possess a single creator would not be proven;
how much less so for cities, rivers, mountains, and the like, which are absolutely heterogeneous from one another?
For indeed, even in the case of objects such as pots, which do have visible creators as their antecedents, a single creator is not perceived.

*vaktavyam* MS: This is a combination of *iti śakyate vaktum* and *iti vaktavyam*.
*°nirvāṇapradhīṇaḥ* MS.
If one should think that their seeds... [MS] ...are [MS]... then one might suppose.
We certainly know the scope of the power of those who possess self-conceit;
yet these mountains and such cannot be created even by people like us, despite our capacity.
Therefore, if a creator of the mountains and such is established, he is established as being entirely distinct from people like us.
Furthermore,
Your Majesty,
being forgetful by nature, does not perceive the context of the matter.
For this is the point at issue here: even by the proponent of God (Īśvaravādin), the distinctness of trees and such from jars and the like must necessarily be admitted;
for how could these [trees], which experience a difference from the works of other persons, be established as being created by a creator who is not distinct from them?

Therefore, if he were now to assert that trees and the like differ from the products of ourselves and others because they cannot be produced by those like us—on the hope of establishing the existence of a person superior to ourselves—then their distinctness would indeed be established. But once this distinctness is established, the pervasion (vyāpti) that all products are the work of a person, which was based on the well-known fact that pots and the like are human products, fails; thus, one must offer a libation of water for the sake of proving God’s existence. [This is the meaning of the verse.]
hi° MS °kṣeṇyaṃ MS °kṣīt MS
[Objection:

Since it is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhitatvāt*), one does not perceive that "mere effect" is pervaded by fire; however, because the person (*puruṣa*) is invisible, its pervasion is not sublated by perception. [Response: This too has been stated by the Teacher of Nyāya (*nyāyācārya*) regarding grass and so forth.
Thus, in this case, there are two alternatives.
Whatever apprehends the pervasion of fire by the effect must be either a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or an invalid one.
If it were a valid means of knowledge, how could it be sublated by another means of knowledge?
On the other hand, if it were invalid, it would be impossible to establish the pervasion of smoke by fire by means of that [invalid cognition].

Now, one might raise the insurmountable and distressing suspicion: "Since there is no distinction in being an effect, why does [the pervasion] not establish the same for anything else as well?"—this is the entry of a difficult-to-overcome doubt regarding the pervasion of smoke by fire. This is what [the author] addresses.
[The reading] *trastara* [is found] in MS;
now, if only a specific effect were invariably concomitant with fire, there would be no determination that an effect of a different class is pervaded by fire.
The most excellent desire of one's own.

In that case, only a specific effect is invariably concomitant with a person; therefore, there is no determination that [the effect] is pervaded by a person because it belongs to a different class. Thus, the introduction of the arguments regarding sublation (*bādha*) and non-sublation by perception is not particularly sound.

If the pervasion between the probandum and the probans were established through mere observation and non-observation due to our own incapacity rather than reality, then it would be improper to describe the pervasion of "mere effect" by "having a person as its antecedent," for those who lack a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).
Since grass and other things are observed to arise even when human activity is not seen,
if you claim that [the arising] is due to an obstruction, then even in that case, it is not proper to describe a pervasion (vyāpti) such that every effect is preceded by a person,
because that very obstruction remains unestablished; enough of this prolixity.
Therefore, it is established that this [world] is without an agent. *akṣeyaḥ* MS.
Therefore, for the sake of the meaning of the measure [of time], [the suffix] *iti* is used; [this applies] to those who have passed away, are passing away, or will pass away.
